Note.description: A page in the garden — a paper summary, a symptom log, a session note, an index. The only type that owns prose on the site.

Session.description: A dated event in the case: a self-administered test, a therapy conversation, a clinical appointment, a deliberate journalling pass. The unit of 'what we did and when'.

Symptom.description: An experienced pattern being tracked — described phenomenologically, not diagnostically.

Instrument.description: A measurement tool: a screener, a questionnaire, a cognitive task, a lab panel, a wearable metric.

Finding.description: A concrete result produced by a Session — a score, a clinician's observation, a lab value. Facts about the case, distinct from what they might mean.

Intervention.description: Something deliberately changed and tracked over time: medication, sleep protocol, therapy, exercise, caffeine, environment.

Mechanism.description: A named cognitive/neural construct the notebook reuses: response inhibition, statistical learning, mind-wandering, executive function.

Hypothesis.description: A load-bearing assertion the notebook is trying to defend or falsify. Never a diagnosis — always something that can be pressure-tested.

Question.description: An open problem the notebook is working on; can gate a Note, a Hypothesis, or a next Session.

Paper.description: An external work cited: journal article, preprint, book, clinical guideline.

Tension.description: A competing-explanation or trade-off held open on purpose — e.g. ADHD vs. anxiety as the source of the same symptom. Reified so it cannot quietly resolve itself.

Status.description: Lifecycle status (a hub-transit type: reachable but never traversed through).

partOf.description: Note belongs to a parent Note (section index).

covers.description: This note is where the thing is written up.

measures.description: Instrument is designed to measure this symptom domain or construct.

administeredIn.description: Instrument was administered during this session.

observedIn.description: Symptom was reported/observed in this session.

precedes.description: Session comes before another session — the timeline spine.

mayExplain.description: Candidate explanation for an experience or result. HYPOTHETICAL by construction — never a diagnosis.

affects.description: Intervention is being tracked for its effect on this.

derivesFrom.description: X is built on / specialises Y.

documentedIn.description: The case fact is written up in this note.

definedIn.description: Mechanism has its primary development in this note.

cites.description: Note cites a paper (a deliberate act, never inferred from prose).

dependsOn.description: Hypothesis rests on another hypothesis, on a question resolving a particular way, or on a finding holding up.

supports.description: Paper supports this hypothesis/mechanism. The edge carries the verbatim quote + page locator + confidence + rationale, so a fact and its justification travel together.

pressureTests.description: Paper challenges/qualifies this hypothesis/mechanism. Same evidence payload.

confounds.description: A rival explanation that must be ruled out before the hypothesis can stand. The honesty predicate of this ontology.

tensionWith.description: In unresolved tension with (both endpoints stay live).

supersedes.description: Replaces a prior version — later screening supersedes an earlier one, a revised hypothesis supersedes its draft.

flagsOpenQuestion.description: Flags an open question the node rests on.

wikiLinks.description: Wiki-style link parsed from prose. Navigation only — kept out of the argument graph.

structural.description: Where a thing sits: containment, coverage, what measures what.

temporal.description: The case timeline: what happened when, in what order, and what it produced.

causal.description: What might explain or affect what. Always hypothetical in this corpus.

provenance.description: Where a thing came from: which note records it, which paper, which author.

dialectical.description: What is contested: evidence, confounds, contradictions, supersession, open questions.

weak.description: Casual cross-links for navigation only — deliberately kept out of the argument graph.

nodes.label: 2026-07-26 — ASRS v1.1 self-screening & reflection
nodes.summary: Took the ASRS v1.1 (WHO-developed adult ADHD screener) and reflected on presentations and the 'calm outside, churning inside' pattern with a therapist who is themselves diagnosed with ADHD.

nodes.label: ASRS v1.1 (Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale)
nodes.summary: 18-item WHO-developed screener. Part A (6 items, cutoff ≥4) determines the screen; Part B (12 items) characterises symptom load. Deliberately tuned for sensitivity, so a positive screen is a reason to evaluate, not a diagnosis.

nodes.label: Cognitive Trade-off Task (ASRT + Go/No-Go)
nodes.summary: The paradigm used by Horváth et al. 2026: an Alternating Serial Reaction Time Task carrying a hidden probabilistic sequence (statistical learning) with an embedded Go/No-Go component (response inhibition), so both are measured at once rather than in isolation.

nodes.label: Continuous performance test (CPT / QbTest)
nodes.summary: Sustained-attention task requiring responses to targets and withholding to non-targets over a long, monotonous session. Indexes vigilance, inhibition and reaction-time variability; sensitive to ADHD but not diagnostically specific.

nodes.label: Stop-signal / go-no-go task
nodes.summary: Measures the ability to cancel an already-initiated response (the stop-signal reaction time) — the cleanest isolation of response inhibition.

nodes.label: Delay-discounting / choice-delay task
nodes.summary: Choices between smaller-sooner and larger-later rewards, quantifying how steeply delayed value is discounted — the motivational/delay-aversion pathway.

nodes.label: Working-memory task (n-back / span)
nodes.summary: n-back and complex-span paradigms indexing the capacity to hold and manipulate information over short intervals.

nodes.label: SWAN rating scale
nodes.summary: Strengths and Weaknesses of ADHD-symptoms and Normal-behavior scale: rates each symptom on a symmetric −3 to +3 range so both tails are measured, yielding roughly normally distributed population scores.

nodes.label: CAARS (Conners Adult ADHD Rating Scales)
nodes.summary: Norm-referenced adult ADHD rating scale scored as T-scores against a population sample; the T≥65 cutoff trades sensitivity for specificity.

nodes.label: BAARS-IV (Barkley Adult ADHD Rating Scale)
nodes.summary: DSM-anchored adult ADHD rating scale with current and childhood-symptom subscales, self- or observer-administered.

nodes.label: PID-5 (Disinhibition domain)
nodes.summary: Dimensional maladaptive-trait inventory; its Disinhibition domain (and Distractibility facet) places a person on the HiTOP disinhibited-externalizing spectrum rather than in the ADHD category.

nodes.label: Internal Restlessness Scale (IRS)
nodes.summary: Self-report scale (Weyandt et al., 2003) that operationalises the subjective/mental restlessness adults with ADHD report in place of overt motor hyperactivity; four factors — internal distractibility, internal impulsivity, internal restlessness, internal disorganization.

nodes.label: DIVA-5 (Diagnostic Interview for ADHD in Adults)
nodes.summary: Structured clinical interview that walks each DSM ADHD symptom across childhood and adulthood with concrete real-life examples, designed to be supplemented by a collateral informant. The instrument a full evaluation uses — distinct from the ASRS screen — though still a clinician tool, not a stand-alone test.

nodes.label: ASRS v1.1 Part A: 4/6 — positive screen
nodes.summary: Landed exactly at the cutoff on the six-item screener that determines the result. Part A is the most predictive component. Screening only — not a diagnosis.

nodes.label: ASRS v1.1 Part B: 6/12 supplementary symptoms
nodes.summary: Part B has no threshold; it describes which symptoms show up. Six indicates a meaningful additional symptom load, backing the Part A result.

nodes.label: No formal diagnosis as of 2026-07-26
nodes.summary: State of the record: a positive screen only. Everything downstream is hypothesis.

nodes.label: Disruptive internal state — calm outside, churning inside
nodes.summary: Outwardly calm and not fidgety, but a racing, unsettled mind — the DSM 'driven as if by a motor' item experienced mentally rather than behaviourally. The often-missed pattern in inattentive-leaning adults.

nodes.label: Inattentive pattern — sustaining focus, distractibility
nodes.summary: Consistent with a positive ASRS Part A and a lean toward the inattentive presentation.

nodes.label: Acting before thinking / impulsivity items
nodes.summary: Endorsed on the ASRS; the axis the Horváth paper probes directly via response inhibition.

nodes.label: Stimulant medication (methylphenidate / amphetamines)
nodes.summary: First-line pharmacological treatment for ADHD with the largest symptom-reduction effects. Listed here as an option on the table, not a treatment started — nothing is in the personal record. Its diagnostic relevance is a caution: because stimulants improve attention in people without ADHD too, feeling better on a trial would not confirm the diagnosis.

nodes.label: Cognitive behavioural therapy for adult ADHD
nodes.summary: Structured skills-based psychotherapy targeting organisation, planning and impulse control in adults with ADHD; meta-analytic effects comparable to well-established child behavioural treatments. An option on the table, not started.

nodes.label: Mindfulness-based therapy
nodes.summary: Attention-training and acceptance-based practice studied as an adjunct for ADHD, with moderate meta-analytic effects on inattention and hyperactivity/impulsivity. Promising but tentatively evidenced; an option on the table, not started.

nodes.label: Response inhibition
nodes.summary: The capacity to withhold a prepared response — indexed by No-Go accuracy. Consistently weaker at higher ADHD-trait load, even below clinical thresholds.

nodes.label: Statistical learning
nodes.summary: Implicit extraction of environmental regularities — the habit-learning system. Indexed by faster responses to high-probability triplets.

nodes.label: Inhibition–learning antagonism (competition hypothesis)
nodes.summary: The trade-off in which weaker inhibitory control normally buys stronger statistical learning. The paper's central object of study.

nodes.label: ADHD as a trait continuum
nodes.summary: The dimensional view: ADHD-like traits are distributed across the general population, and neurocognitive shifts appear before symptoms reach clinical significance. The frame that makes a screening score meaningful without a diagnosis.

nodes.label: Cue as motivational magnet (sign-tracking)
nodes.summary: Borrowed from animal sign-tracker/goal-tracker work: at high trait load the cue itself captures behaviour and top-down systems cannot override it — the authors' proposed reason the learning advantage breaks down.

nodes.label: Mind-wandering
nodes.summary: Spontaneous shift of attention from external demands to internally generated thought; offered as a second, transdiagnostic candidate mechanism.

nodes.label: Anxiety-driven arousal
nodes.summary: Chronic anxious arousal produces internal churn that is phenomenologically near-identical to internal hyperactivity, and frequently co-occurs with ADHD. The single most important thing to rule out here.

nodes.label: Sleep debt / disrupted sleep
nodes.summary: Insufficient or fragmented sleep degrades attention and produces restlessness — a mimic that must be excluded before attributing symptoms to ADHD.

nodes.label: Mood disturbance (depression / chronic stress)
nodes.summary: Depression and chronic stress produce concentration difficulty and inner agitation. Another mimic on the differential.

nodes.label: Sustained attention / vigilance
nodes.summary: The capacity to maintain attention on a task over time. A mechanism-level axis, indexed by continuous performance tests; lapses show up as reaction-time variability.

nodes.label: Working memory
nodes.summary: Holding and manipulating information over short intervals. One of the dissociable neurocognitive routes to ADHD-like presentation; indexed by n-back and complex-span tasks.

nodes.label: Reward processing / delay aversion
nodes.summary: The motivational pathway: an aversion to waiting and steeper discounting of delayed rewards. Partly independent of the inhibitory route; indexed by delay-discounting paradigms.

nodes.label: Arousal / state regulation
nodes.summary: Regulation of physiological and cognitive arousal. The axis ADHD shares most with its mimics — anxiety, sleep debt and mood all perturb it, which is why they overlap ADHD at the phenotype. The cognitive-energetic model defines its energetic pools as responsive to stress, sleep and noise, so the overlap is by construction; the putatively ADHD-specific part is the regulation, evidenced by condition-dependence.

nodes.label: Excessive spontaneous mind-wandering
nodes.summary: Constant, topic-unstable internal mental activity, proposed to arise from altered default-mode deactivation and DMN–executive interaction. Measured by the MEWS; targets the form rather than the content of thought. Its ADHD-specificity is contested — it also tracks anxiety.

nodes.label: Reaction-time variability
nodes.summary: Intra-individual variability in response speed — a robust and heavily replicated ADHD marker, but not specific to ADHD relative to other clinical groups.

nodes.label: Temporal processing / timing
nodes.summary: Perception and reproduction of time intervals. A third dissociable component in multiple-pathway models, independent of inhibition and delay aversion.

nodes.label: Cognitive disengagement syndrome (formerly sluggish cognitive tempo)
nodes.summary: A construct of attention decoupling from the external context — staring, daydreaming, mental fogginess, slowed thinking and hypoactivity. Distinct from ADHD inattention in factor-analytic work and more strongly tied to internalizing (depression) than to hyperactivity/impulsivity, which makes it a rival reading of a foggy, disengaged 'internal state' rather than an anxious, churning one.

nodes.label: Emotional dysregulation
nodes.summary: Difficulty modulating emotional responses — lability, low frustration tolerance, quick temper, slow return to baseline. Prevalent across the ADHD lifespan and a major driver of impairment, proposed to arise from deficits in attention to emotional stimuli. It overlaps anxiety and mood by construction, so it both deepens the ADHD phenotype and blurs the boundary with the mimics; whether it is core to ADHD or a distinct dimension is unsettled.

nodes.label: Default-mode network interference
nodes.summary: A neurobiological model in which spontaneous low-frequency default-mode-network activity, normally suppressed during tasks, intrudes into task-positive processing and produces periodic attentional lapses. Proposed as a substrate for reaction-time variability and inattention, it links the mind-wandering and vigilance axes to a specific network rather than a single region.

nodes.label: My disruptive internal state is ADHD-driven rather than anxiety-, sleep-, or mood-driven
nodes.summary: The load-bearing personal hypothesis. Three rival mechanisms confound it and none has been ruled out; it cannot advance until the internal state is described concretely.

nodes.label: My ASRS result places me on the ADHD trait continuum rather than in a yes/no category
nodes.summary: Framing rather than diagnosis: a Part A score at the cutoff situates me somewhere on a spectrum the literature treats dimensionally.

nodes.label: ADHD's latent structure is dimensional (a continuum), not a discrete taxon
nodes.summary: Taxometric analyses of ADHD symptom data repeatedly fail to recover a category boundary and instead fit a continuous latent dimension. Contested: some analyses recover categorical structure within clinical samples.

nodes.label: Clinical ADHD is the quantitative extreme of a continuously distributed, heritable trait
nodes.summary: Twin and molecular-genetic evidence that the same aetiological factors operate across the whole symptom range, so the diagnosis marks a position on a continuum rather than a distinct condition.

nodes.label: The DSM symptom-count threshold is an arbitrary cut on a continuum with no natural breakpoint
nodes.summary: Impairment and quality of life decline linearly across the trait range with no discontinuity, so any diagnostic cutoff is a clinical convention. Held live by the counter-argument that unbounded threshold-lowering risks overdiagnosis and net harm.

nodes.label: Major dimensional frameworks (RDoC, HiTOP, the p-factor) place ADHD within continuous, transdiagnostic spectra
nodes.summary: The leading post-DSM classification programmes are all dimensional and locate ADHD on graded spectra (externalizing/disinhibition, general psychopathology) rather than in a discrete box.

nodes.label: A positive ASRS screen warrants a full clinical evaluation
nodes.summary: The actionable claim. Holds regardless of how the ADHD-vs-mimics question resolves — the evaluation is what resolves it.

nodes.label: Higher ADHD-like traits are associated with weaker response inhibition
nodes.summary: Research-side claim, replicated by the Horváth study in a non-clinical sample and under dual-task load.

nodes.label: Rising ADHD-trait load progressively flattens the inhibition–learning trade-off
nodes.summary: The paper's core result: the compensatory learning advantage that normally accompanies weak inhibition breaks down at the high end of the trait continuum.

nodes.label: Inattention and hyperactivity/impulsivity are distinct but strongly correlated, not orthogonal
nodes.summary: At the phenotype level the two DSM domains share a dominant general factor (latent r ≈ .68–.78); a bifactor structure fits best, so the domains are oblique rather than independent axes.

nodes.label: Rating-based and task-based measures of the same construct are only weakly related
nodes.summary: Questionnaire and performance measures of executive function correlate at about median r = .19 and assess different levels of cognition — so the two instrument families are near-orthogonal, not interchangeable.

nodes.label: ADHD arises through dissociable neurocognitive pathways, present in some individuals but not others
nodes.summary: Inhibitory, delay/reward and timing deficits are independent components whose co-occurrence is no greater than chance, and no single deficit is universal — the mechanism level is genuinely near-orthogonal.

nodes.label: No single instrument is diagnostic; valid assessment is multi-method across levels
nodes.summary: Ratings and tasks disagree, the best objective tasks are not decisive, and robust markers like reaction-time variability are not ADHD-specific — so discriminating ADHD (and its mimics) requires a multi-method evaluation, not one measure.

nodes.label: ADHD measures separate ADHD from healthy controls, but not from the mimics
nodes.summary: Ratings and tasks alike discriminate ADHD from typically developing controls, yet lose their edge against other clinical conditions — anxiety, mood, OCD — so no single instrument can rule out the differential. The measurement-side root of the ADHD-vs-anxiety tension.

nodes.label: Most adult-identified ADHD is late-identified rather than genuinely late-onset
nodes.summary: Birth cohorts found adult and childhood ADHD groups barely overlap, but careful repeated assessment excludes ~95% of screen-positive late-onset cases; survivors show childhood symptoms masked by cognitive strength. Compensation plus rising demand, not new onset.

nodes.label: The course of ADHD fluctuates rather than simply persisting or remitting
nodes.summary: Most of the MTA sample showed waxing and waning persistence and remission rather than stable persistence or recovery, making person-environment fit the appropriate frame — the temporal counterpart of the dimensional argument.

nodes.label: The ADHD sex ratio largely reflects referral and ascertainment, not underlying prevalence
nodes.summary: Clinic ratios far exceed community ratios in the same populations, high-symptom girls are diagnosed less often than high-symptom boys, and the gap narrows to ~1.5:1 in adulthood — the signature of under-detection rather than a true prevalence difference.

nodes.label: The arousal/state-regulation axis is shared with the mimics by construction, not by coincidence
nodes.summary: The cognitive-energetic model defines its energetic pools as responsive to stress, sleep-wake cycle and noise — so sleep debt and anxiety move the very variable ADHD is hypothesised to dysregulate. What may be ADHD-specific is the regulation, evidenced by condition-dependence.

nodes.label: Excessive mind-wandering is transdiagnostic rather than an ADHD marker
nodes.summary: Mind-wandering tracked anxiety independently of ADHD diagnosis and showed no categorical ADHD/non-ADHD difference, while correlating with inattention dimensionally — and it mediates ADHD symptoms' relationship to anxiety and depression.

nodes.label: Sleep debt is a strong rival for inattention but a weak one for internal restlessness
nodes.summary: Experimental sleep restriction reliably degrades attention and emotional lability in healthy people, but no experiment has shown it induces hyperactivity or impulsivity — narrowing which half of the picture sleep can explain.

nodes.label: Onset, trajectory and counterfactual — not symptom intensity — discriminate ADHD from anxiety
nodes.summary: Because both conditions produce internal restlessness and the rating items measuring it are partly anxiety items, the discriminating evidence is structural: whether the restlessness predates any anxiety, persists in its absence, is situational or constant, and whether its content is worry or topic-shifting.

nodes.label: The 'calm outside, churning inside' state is internalized hyperactivity — subjective restlessness — not overt motor hyperactivity
nodes.summary: DSM allows adult hyperactivity to present as subjective restlessness, and adults with ADHD report mental restlessness in place of fidgeting; the IRS measures it and separates ADHD from non-ADHD students. This reframes the internal state as the adult form of the hyperactive axis — but the same internalized presentation is where anxiety is hardest to distinguish from ADHD.

nodes.label: Cognitive disengagement (daydreamy, foggy, mentally slow) is a construct distinct from ADHD inattention and more tied to internalizing
nodes.summary: Factor-analytic and meta-analytic work separates cognitive disengagement syndrome (formerly SCT) from ADHD inattention and links it more to depression/internalizing than to hyperactivity/impulsivity. If the internal state is foggy and disengaged rather than restless, CDS — not ADHD hyperactivity — may be the better description, and it points toward the mood differential.

nodes.label: ADHD and anxiety co-occur far above chance across the lifespan
nodes.summary: Adult ADHD is highly comorbid with other DSM disorders, up to ~80% carry at least one, and ~25% of children with ADHD have an anxiety disorder. High comorbidity is why the ADHD-vs-anxiety differential is genuinely hard rather than a technicality — the two really do travel together.

nodes.label: Emotional dysregulation is a core feature of ADHD, not merely a comorbidity
nodes.summary: Emotion dysregulation is prevalent across the ADHD lifespan and a major contributor to impairment, and has been called a distinctive attribute of adult ADHD. But its status is explicitly unsettled: it is equally consistent with being a correlated-but-distinct dimension or a separate entity, so 'core' is one reading among three.

nodes.label: The DSM childhood-onset requirement is hard to verify from an adult's own recall, so collateral information matters
nodes.summary: DSM needs some symptoms present in childhood, but adult self-recall of childhood ADHD has a positive predictive value near 0.27, and young adults with ADHD tend to underreport. Guidelines therefore lean on contemporaneous records and collateral informants (a parent or partner). This bears directly on a first evaluation in adulthood with no childhood documentation.

nodes.label: A positive response to stimulant medication does not confirm ADHD
nodes.summary: Normal children given dextroamphetamine show the same reduced activity and improved cognition as hyperactive children, so there is no ADHD-specific or 'paradoxical' stimulant response. Improvement on a medication trial is therefore not diagnostic evidence — a treatment-response confound on the personal ADHD hypothesis.

nodes.label: Evidence-based treatments meaningfully reduce adult ADHD symptoms
nodes.summary: Medication (methylphenidate in youth, amphetamines in adults) has the largest short-term effects; CBT for adults reaches effect sizes comparable to well-established child behavioural treatments; mindfulness shows moderate but tentatively-framed benefit. Treatment works — separately from whether a given internal state is ADHD.

nodes.label: ADHD reflects altered function across large-scale brain networks, not a single region or lesion
nodes.summary: The older prefrontal-striatal model has given way to systems-level accounts spanning multiple resting-state networks (frontoparietal, dorsal attention, default, visual). There is no ADHD 'spot' in the brain; the biology is distributed and network-level, which is consistent with a graded, dimensional phenotype rather than a discrete lesion.

nodes.label: Structural brain differences in ADHD are real at the group level but too small to diagnose an individual
nodes.summary: The largest imaging studies (ENIGMA) find real but tiny group differences — subcortical volumes at Cohen's d around -0.1 to -0.2, cortical effects no larger, and no detectable cortical differences at all in adolescents or adults. Group-level signal does not license an individual scan-based diagnosis, and the adult null is especially relevant to a first evaluation in adulthood.

nodes.label: ADHD and autism co-occur far above chance
nodes.summary: Co-occurrence estimates run high (roughly 20–50% of children with ADHD meet ASD criteria and 30–80% of ASD children meet ADHD criteria). DSM-IV had barred diagnosing both, which suppressed research; DSM-5 now permits a dual diagnosis, and the overlap is now openly studied.

nodes.label: ADHD and autism share heritable and neurocognitive substrates
nodes.summary: Family and twin studies support partly shared familial-genetic origins, with candidate pleiotropic genes, and the two share impairments in social and executive functioning. The overlap is not merely superficial symptom sharing but reaches down to partly common causes.

nodes.label: Despite the overlap, ADHD and autism remain distinct diagnostic categories
nodes.summary: Shared genetics and impairments notwithstanding, the phenotypic presentations differ qualitatively and quantitatively enough that reviews conclude the two are sufficiently distinct to warrant separate diagnoses. Overlap at the level of causes does not collapse the clinical distinction.

nodes.label: What does the 'disruptive internal state' actually consist of?
nodes.summary: Racing/jumping thoughts, a physical-but-invisible wound-up feeling, an inability to ever relax, or something else. These feel similar from the inside but point in different directions.
nodes.nextStep: Journal concrete examples as they happen, with time of day and context.

nodes.label: Is the internal restlessness driven by ADHD, anxiety, sleep, mood, or a combination?
nodes.summary: The differential. A good evaluator traces the symptom to its source rather than assuming the ADHD thread.
nodes.nextStep: Bring the differential explicitly to the evaluation; don't let it collapse into a single label.

nodes.label: Where would my ASRS score fall relative to the Horváth sample?
nodes.summary: The paper's sample scored M = 31.66, SD = 10.04 on the 18-item ASRS. My record currently stores Part A/Part B counts, not the summed dimensional score — so the comparison can't yet be made.
nodes.nextStep: Retain the item-level ASRS responses and compute the summed score.

nodes.label: What is the right next clinical step, and with whom?
nodes.summary: GP referral, psychologist, or psychiatrist — and what to bring to make the appointment productive.
nodes.nextStep: Draft a one-page summary for a clinician from the diagnostics note and the symptom log.

nodes.label: ADHD-like traits reshape the balance between inhibitory control and predictive processes
nodes.summary: n = 226 non-clinical sample; Cognitive Trade-off Task measuring response inhibition and statistical learning simultaneously; ADHD traits measured dimensionally with the ASRS v1.1.

nodes.label: Annual Research Review: Categories versus dimensions in the classification and conceptualisation of child and adolescent mental disorders
nodes.venue: Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry, 53(5):469–489
nodes.summary: Canonical review of the category-vs-dimension question in child psychopathology; summarises the ADHD taxometric studies (Haslam 2006, Marcus & Barry 2011) and concludes ADHD is best modelled as a continuum.

nodes.label: Understanding attention deficit hyperactivity disorder as a continuum
nodes.summary: Clinician-facing review arguing ADHD lacks a taxon; neuropsychological performance varies linearly with symptom load with no discontinuity, creating uncertainty about where any intervention threshold should sit.

nodes.label: Does Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder Have a Dimensional Latent Structure? A Taxometric Analysis
nodes.summary: Taxometric analysis of the NICHD sample finding a dimensional latent structure for inattention, hyperactivity/impulsivity and ADHD overall, with stronger validity than dichotomous models.

nodes.label: Genetics of attention deficit hyperactivity disorder
nodes.summary: Review of ADHD genetics; twin and molecular evidence that clinical ADHD is the extreme of a continuous, heritable distribution with shared aetiology across the full symptom range.

nodes.label: Discovery of the first genome-wide significant risk loci for attention deficit/hyperactivity disorder
nodes.summary: First well-powered ADHD GWAS; strong concordance with GWAS of quantitative population symptom measures supports clinical ADHD as an extreme expression of continuous heritable traits.

nodes.label: The World Health Organization Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale (ASRS): a short screening scale for use in the general population
nodes.summary: Development of the ASRS; optimal scoring is an unweighted symptom sum (a dimensional score), with a 6-item Part A retained as a fast screener.

nodes.label: SWAN Scale for ADHD Trait-Based Genetic Research: A Validity and Polygenic Risk Study
nodes.venue: Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry, 60(9):988–997
nodes.summary: Validates the SWAN, a symmetric strengths-to-weaknesses rating that yields roughly normally distributed ADHD-trait scores; argues dichotomising a continuous trait into case/control loses statistical power.

nodes.label: The Factor Structure of ADHD – Different Models, Analyses and Informants in a Bifactor Framework
nodes.venue: Journal of Psychopathology and Behavioral Assessment, 39(1):92–102
nodes.summary: Supports a bifactor structure for ADHD: a dominant general factor plus weak specific inattention and hyperactivity/impulsivity factors.

nodes.label: Research Domain Criteria (RDoC): Toward a New Classification Framework for Research on Mental Disorders
nodes.summary: Founding RDoC commentary; reorganises psychopathology around functional dimensions studied across their full range, including executive- and impulse-control constructs central to ADHD.

nodes.label: The Hierarchical Taxonomy of Psychopathology (HiTOP): A Dimensional Alternative to Traditional Nosologies
nodes.summary: Dimensional classification framework that places ADHD within the (disinhibited) externalizing super-spectrum rather than as a discrete category.

nodes.label: The p Factor: One General Psychopathology Factor in the Structure of Psychiatric Disorders?
nodes.summary: Finds psychopathology is best captured by a single general 'p' dimension paralleling g; ADHD loads via the externalizing pole, reinforcing a graded liability model.

nodes.label: Is ADHD a Dimension or a Category? What Does the Relationship Between ADHD Traits and Psychosocial Quality of Life Tell Us?
nodes.summary: Psychosocial quality of life declines linearly with ADHD-trait level, with no non-linear breakpoint at the high end — direct support for a dimensional model over a category.

nodes.label: Subthreshold Autism and ADHD: A Brief Narrative Review for Frontline Clinicians
nodes.summary: Narrative review synthesising taxometric, impairment and threshold evidence; documents that sub-threshold ADHD carries wide-ranging functional impairment relative to unaffected peers.

nodes.label: Overdiagnosis of Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder in Children and Adolescents: A Systematic Scoping Review
nodes.summary: Scoping review of 334 studies finding convincing evidence that ADHD is overdiagnosed; for milder cases the harms of diagnosis may outweigh the benefits — a caution against unbounded threshold-lowering.

nodes.label: Childhood attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder as an extreme of a continuous trait: a quantitative genetic study of 8,500 twin pairs
nodes.venue: Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry, 53(1):73–80
nodes.summary: Flagship twin study reporting near-identical group heritability at diagnostic and screening cutoffs — ADHD as the quantitative extreme of a continuous trait.

nodes.label: Dimensional and Categorical Approaches to Understanding Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder: New Frontiers in Translational Research
nodes.venue: Biological Psychiatry: Cognitive Neuroscience and Neuroimaging, 3(8):652–653
nodes.summary: Counter-point to the dimensional consensus: reports taxometric outcomes more consistent with a categorical structure within ADHD samples and a dimensional structure in typically developing groups.

nodes.label: The factor structure of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder in schoolchildren
nodes.venue: medRxiv preprint (later Research in Developmental Disabilities)
nodes.summary: Reports the latent correlation between the inattention and hyperactivity/impulsivity factors (0.78 school / 0.68 clinical) and finds a bifactor model — strong general factor plus weak specific factors — fits best.

nodes.label: Practitioner Review: Do performance-based measures and ratings of executive function assess the same construct?
nodes.venue: Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry, 54(2):131–143
nodes.summary: Review of 20 studies finding rating-based and performance-based measures of executive function correlate only weakly (median r = .19) and assess different underlying constructs.

nodes.label: Causal heterogeneity in attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder: do we need neuropsychologically impaired subtypes?
nodes.summary: Argues that group neuropsychological deficits in ADHD reflect only a subgroup — for any given mechanism, only a subset of behaviourally defined cases is impaired.

nodes.label: Beyond the dual pathway model: evidence for the dissociation of timing, inhibitory, and delay-related impairments in ADHD
nodes.venue: Journal of the American Academy of Child & Adolescent Psychiatry, 49(4):345–355
nodes.summary: Finds inhibitory, temporal-processing and delay-related deficits are independent neuropsychological components whose co-occurrence in ADHD is no greater than chance — dissociable pathways.

nodes.label: Reaction time variability in ADHD: a meta-analytic review of 319 studies
nodes.summary: Meta-analysis establishing greater reaction-time variability in ADHD (g = 0.76 children, 0.46 adults) while showing it is not specific to ADHD relative to other clinical groups.

nodes.label: The clinical utility of the continuous performance test and objective measures of activity for diagnosing and monitoring ADHD in children: a systematic review
nodes.summary: Systematic review finding mixed, non-decisive evidence for using continuous performance tests to support ADHD diagnosis and medication decisions.

nodes.label: A review of the validity of laboratory cognitive tasks used to assess symptoms of ADHD
nodes.summary: Concludes that even the best-supported cognitive tasks (CPT, choice-delay, stop-signal) need further validation before use beyond experimental purposes.

nodes.label: Validity of the executive function theory of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder: a meta-analytic review
nodes.summary: Landmark meta-analysis: executive-function deficits in ADHD are of moderate effect size and not universal — neither necessary nor sufficient.

nodes.label: A comprehensive assessment of memory, delay aversion, timing, inhibition, decision making and variability in ADHD
nodes.summary: For each cognitive domain, only a minority of children with ADHD (roughly 18–36%) show a deficit — quantifying neurocognitive heterogeneity across six pathways.

nodes.label: Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder and Monetary Delay Discounting: A Meta-Analysis of Case-Control Studies
nodes.venue: Biological Psychiatry: Cognitive Neuroscience and Neuroimaging, 1(4):316–325
nodes.summary: Meta-analysis finding individuals with ADHD discount delayed monetary rewards more steeply than controls — the motivational/reward pathway.

nodes.label: A review of behavioural rating scales for the assessment of ADHD among adults in research
nodes.summary: Reviews adult ADHD rating scales (incl. CAARS, BAARS-IV); notes scales should not be the sole basis for diagnosis and that combining interviews, CPTs and scales maximises accuracy.

nodes.label: Diagnosing ADHD
nodes.venue: CHADD — National Resource Center on ADHD (CDC cooperative agreement)
nodes.summary: Patient-facing clinical guidance stating there is no single test for ADHD and that a comprehensive, multi-source evaluation is required.

nodes.label: Unraveling the optimum latent structure of ADHD: evidence supporting ICD and HiTOP frameworks
nodes.summary: Locates ADHD within HiTOP as dimensions (inattention, hyperactivity, impulsivity) under the disinhibited externalizing spectrum rather than as a single category.

nodes.label: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis: Clinical Utility of Continuous Performance Tests for the Identification of ADHD
nodes.venue: Journal of the American Academy of Child & Adolescent Psychiatry, 63(2):154–171
nodes.summary: Meta-analysis: CPTs differentiate ADHD from non-ADHD only modestly (pooled sensitivity 0.75, specificity 0.71) and should be used only within a comprehensive diagnostic process.

nodes.label: ADHD and behavioral inhibition: a meta-analytic review of the stop-signal paradigm
nodes.summary: Meta-analysis finding that stop-signal differences in ADHD reflect a generalized attention/processing deficit rather than a specific behavioural-inhibition failure.

nodes.label: Are we measuring ADHD or anxiety? Examining the factor structure and discriminant validity of the ASRS in an adult anxiety disorder population
nodes.summary: In an adult anxiety sample, several ASRS hyperactivity items loaded more strongly onto anxiety than ADHD; the scale captured non-ADHD symptoms and is susceptible to over-reporting.

nodes.label: Is adult ADHD a childhood-onset neurodevelopmental disorder? Evidence from a four-decade longitudinal cohort study
nodes.summary: Dunedin birth cohort: childhood-ADHD and adult-ADHD groups were virtually non-overlapping, and the adult group showed neither childhood neuropsychological deficits nor polygenic risk for childhood ADHD.

nodes.label: Evaluation of the persistence, remission, and emergence of ADHD in young adulthood
nodes.summary: E-Risk twin cohort: 67.5% of young adults with ADHD had never met criteria in childhood; the late-onset group had higher childhood IQ and fewer externalizing problems.

nodes.label: ADHD trajectories from childhood to young adulthood: evidence from a birth cohort supporting a late-onset syndrome
nodes.summary: Pelotas birth cohort: only 17.2% of childhood cases persisted and only 12.6% of adult cases had childhood ADHD; the authors propose two syndromes with distinct trajectories.

nodes.label: Late-onset ADHD reconsidered with comprehensive repeated assessments between ages 10 and 25
nodes.summary: Using eight repeated multi-informant assessments, ~95% of screen-positive late-onset cases were excluded on careful diagnosis; survivors are reframed as late-identified rather than late-onset.

nodes.label: Variable patterns of remission from ADHD in the Multimodal Treatment Study of ADHD
nodes.summary: Across 16 years, only 9.1% recovered and 10.8% were stably persistent; 63.8% showed fluctuating persistence and remission, motivating a person-environment fit framework.

nodes.label: ADHD in DSM-5: a field trial in a large, representative sample of 18- to 19-year-old adults
nodes.summary: Supports five inattention symptoms as the optimal adult cut-off while estimating a 27% increase in expected young-adult prevalence from DSM-IV to DSM-5.

nodes.label: The prevalence of adult attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder: a global systematic review and meta-analysis
nodes.summary: Persistent adult ADHD 2.58% vs symptomatic adult ADHD 6.76% — a ~2.6x difference driven purely by whether childhood onset is required; both decline with age.

nodes.label: ADHD diagnosis, treatment, and telehealth use in adults — National Center for Health Statistics Rapid Surveys System
nodes.venue: MMWR Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report, 73(40):890–895
nodes.summary: 6.0% of US adults had a current ADHD diagnosis in 2023; 55.9% were diagnosed at age 18 or older — late identification is the majority pathway.

nodes.label: Sex and age differences in ADHD symptoms and diagnoses: implications for DSM-V and ICD-11
nodes.venue: Journal of the American Academy of Child & Adolescent Psychiatry, 49(3):217–228
nodes.summary: Community-ascertained male:female ratio of 2.28:1, well below clinic-based ratios, indicating females are underdiagnosed in the community.

nodes.label: Sex differences in predicting ADHD clinical diagnosis and pharmacological treatment
nodes.summary: Swedish cohort: diagnosed ratio 2.5:1 vs symptom-criteria ratio 1.8:1; externalizing behaviour drives referral, and females are missed without it.

nodes.label: Annual Research Review: ADHD in girls and women — underrepresentation, longitudinal processes, and key directions
nodes.venue: Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry, 63(4):484–496
nodes.summary: Reviews presentation differences, the narrowing adult sex ratio, compensation/masking, and the male-referenced bias of ADHD symptom lists.

nodes.label: The prevalence of DSM-IV attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder: a meta-analytic review
nodes.summary: The inattentive presentation is most common in the population, but combined-type individuals are more likely to be referred for services — a structural referral filter.

nodes.label: Gender differences in objective and subjective measures of ADHD among clinic-referred children
nodes.summary: Documents the 2:1 to 10:1 range of reported sex ratios and that higher ratios come specifically from clinical rather than population-based samples.

nodes.label: Bias by gender: exploring gender-based differences in the endorsement of ADHD symptoms and impairment among adult patients
nodes.summary: Notes that only 21% of participants in the DSM-5/ICD-11 ADHD field trials were girls, so diagnostic tools were largely not designed with women in mind.

nodes.label: Modeling attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder: a critical appraisal of the cognitive-energetic model
nodes.summary: Argues inhibition deficits in ADHD may be partly explained by energetic (activation/effort) dysfunction, while conceding the model needs direct measures of the energetic pools.

nodes.label: A comparison of two models of ADHD: state regulation versus delay aversion
nodes.venue: Doctoral dissertation, Ghent University (ch. based on Metin et al. 2012, Biological Psychiatry 72:990–996)
nodes.summary: Meta-analysis of event-rate effects showing ADHD performance deficits are condition-dependent; also states that the energetic pools are affected by stress, sleep-wake cycle and noise.

nodes.label: Arousal dysregulation and executive dysfunction in attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD)
nodes.summary: Reviews evidence that the ADHD impairment is in the ability to self-regulate arousal rather than a constant under- or over-aroused state, while noting mixed results.

nodes.label: Mind wandering perspective on attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder
nodes.summary: Proposes that altered default-mode deactivation and DMN–executive interaction produce excessive spontaneous mind-wandering underpinning ADHD symptoms.

nodes.label: Validation of the Mind Excessively Wandering Scale and the relationship of mind wandering to impairment in adult ADHD
nodes.summary: Validates the MEWS (sensitivity .9, specificity .9) and finds mind-wandering contributes to impairment independently of core ADHD symptom dimensions.

nodes.label: Mind-wandering, depression, anxiety and ADHD: disentangling the relationship
nodes.summary: Found no mind-wandering difference between ADHD and non-ADHD groups; mind-wandering tracked anxiety instead and 'cannot be considered a hallmark of ADHD'.

nodes.label: Associations of sleep disturbance with ADHD: implications for treatment
nodes.venue: ADHD Attention Deficit and Hyperactivity Disorders, 7(1):1–18
nodes.summary: Sets out four modes of ADHD-sleep interaction including that sleep problems may cause or mimic ADHD, and notes no experiment has shown sleep restriction induces hyperactivity.

nodes.label: Impact of sleep extension and restriction on children's emotional lability and impulsivity
nodes.summary: In healthy children with no sleep or behavioural problems, ~54 minutes of cumulative sleep restriction produced detectable deterioration on blinded teacher ratings.

nodes.label: Sleep restriction and extension in adolescents with ADHD
nodes.venue: Journal of the American Academy of Child & Adolescent Psychiatry, 58(4):433–442
nodes.summary: Experimental evidence that sleep duration is a causal contributor to daytime behaviour in adolescents with ADHD; hyperactivity-impulsivity was lower under restriction.

nodes.label: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) in adults: evidence base, uncertainties and controversies
nodes.summary: Comprehensive review of adult ADHD; sets out onset, trajectory and mechanism as the three tests for differential diagnosis, and describes adult hyperactivity as inner restlessness.

nodes.label: Inhibitory control and psychopathology: a meta-analysis of studies using the stop signal task
nodes.venue: Journal of the International Neuropsychological Society, 16(6):1064–1076
nodes.summary: Medium stop-signal deficits across ADHD (g=0.62), OCD (g=0.77) and schizophrenia (g=0.69) — inhibition impairment is transdiagnostic, and OCD's exceeds ADHD's.

nodes.label: The Internal Restlessness Scale: performance of college students with and without ADHD
nodes.summary: Develops the Internal Restlessness Scale (IRS) to measure the mental/subjective restlessness that adults with ADHD report in place of overt motor hyperactivity; ADHD college students score significantly higher, and the scale shows a four-factor structure.

nodes.label: Practical considerations for the evaluation and management of Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) in adults
nodes.summary: Clinician-facing review of adult ADHD; notes that in adulthood hyperactivity is more often internalized and that inattention can be masked by anxiety or obsessive-like compensation — directly relevant to the internal-restlessness / anxiety differential.

nodes.label: The Internal, External, and Diagnostic Validity of Sluggish Cognitive Tempo: A Meta-Analysis and Critical Review
nodes.venue: Journal of the American Academy of Child & Adolescent Psychiatry, 55(3):163–178
nodes.summary: First meta-analysis of sluggish cognitive tempo (SCT): across >19,000 individuals 13 SCT items load on an SCT factor separable from ADHD; SCT correlates more with internalizing than with hyperactivity/impulsivity and predicts impairment — evidence for a construct distinct from ADHD inattention.

nodes.label: Report of a Work Group on Sluggish Cognitive Tempo: Key Research Directions and a Consensus Change in Terminology to Cognitive Disengagement Syndrome
nodes.venue: Journal of the American Academy of Child & Adolescent Psychiatry, 62(6):629–645
nodes.summary: Consensus paper renaming SCT to cognitive disengagement syndrome (CDS); defines it as cognitive disengagement/decoupling of attention (staring, daydreaming, mental fogginess) plus hypoactivity, empirically distinct from ADHD inattention and linked to depression, with data across the lifespan.

nodes.label: The prevalence and correlates of adult ADHD in the United States: results from the National Comorbidity Survey Replication
nodes.summary: Nationally representative US survey (NCS-R): current adult ADHD prevalence 4.4%, highly comorbid with other DSM-IV disorders and substantially impairing; most cases untreated though often treated for the comorbidities — evidence the disorder frequently hides behind its co-occurring conditions.

nodes.label: Emotion dysregulation in attention deficit hyperactivity disorder
nodes.summary: Review concluding emotion dysregulation is prevalent across the ADHD lifespan and a major source of impairment, arising from attention-to-emotion deficits in a striato-amygdalo-medial-prefrontal network; explicitly lays out three competing models of how it relates to ADHD (distinct dimension / core feature / separate entity).

nodes.label: Adult ADHD and comorbid disorders: clinical implications of a dimensional approach
nodes.summary: Review of adult ADHD comorbidity: up to 80% have a coexisting psychiatric disorder (most often mood/anxiety), overlapping symptoms complicate diagnosis, and a spectrum/dimensional framing plus treat-the-most-impairing-first is advocated; emotional dysregulation described as a distinctive attribute of adult ADHD.

nodes.label: A conceptual review of the comorbidity of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder and anxiety: implications for future research and practice
nodes.summary: Conceptual review of ADHD–anxiety comorbidity (~25% of children with ADHD have an anxiety disorder); examines methodological and substantive causes including temperament, genetics and the temporal relations between the two, and argues progress needs more precise phenotypic classification of ADHD.

nodes.label: The World Federation of ADHD International Consensus Statement: 208 Evidence-based conclusions about the disorder
nodes.summary: Consensus statement (79 authors, 27 countries) distilling ADHD evidence into 208 numbered conclusions; Conclusion 14 states ADHD can only be diagnosed by a licensed clinician via interview and not by rating scales, neuropsychological tests or imaging alone.

nodes.label: Updated European Consensus Statement on diagnosis and treatment of adult ADHD
nodes.summary: European consensus (63 experts) on adult ADHD assessment and treatment: the clinical interview is essential and covers childhood and adult symptoms/impairment; a collateral informant is of great value where retrospective recall is poor; a four-symptom adult cut-off is endorsed.

nodes.label: Accuracy of adult recall of childhood attention deficit hyperactivity disorder
nodes.summary: Prospective 16-year follow-up testing whether adults accurately recall childhood ADHD: positive predictive value of retrospective self-report was only 0.27, so most retrospective childhood diagnoses are invalid — underscoring the need for contemporaneous or collateral childhood information.

nodes.label: When diagnosing ADHD in young adults emphasize informant reports, DSM items, and impairment
nodes.venue: Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology, 80(6):1052–1061
nodes.summary: Childhood-diagnosed sample (N=321) showing parent report is more diagnostically sensitive than self-report: young adults with ADHD underreport symptoms while controls overreport, with no added benefit to combining self-report with parent report — argues for weighting informants and impairment.

nodes.label: Dextroamphetamine: cognitive and behavioral effects in normal prepubertal boys
nodes.summary: Double-blind study of a single dextroamphetamine dose in 14 normal prepubertal boys: they showed reduced motor activity and improved cognitive performance just like hyperactive children, casting doubt on the idea of a stimulant response specific to ADHD — the classic evidence that medication response is not diagnostic.

nodes.label: Comparative efficacy and tolerability of medications for ADHD in children, adolescents, and adults: a systematic review and network meta-analysis
nodes.summary: Network meta-analysis of 133 double-blind RCTs across the lifespan; taking efficacy and safety together, supports methylphenidate as first choice in children/adolescents and amphetamines in adults for short-term ADHD treatment, while flagging that long-term effects are under-studied.

nodes.label: Meta-analysis of cognitive-behavioral treatments for adult ADHD
nodes.venue: Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology, 85(7):737–750
nodes.summary: Meta-analysis of 32 CBT studies (up to 896 adults): medium-to-large pre-post effects and small-to-medium effects versus control, comparable to well-established behavioural treatments for children — evidence that non-pharmacological treatment meaningfully reduces adult ADHD symptoms.

nodes.label: The Effectiveness of Mindfulness-Based Therapies for ADHD: A Meta-Analytic Review
nodes.summary: Meta-analysis of mindfulness-based therapies for ADHD: moderate effect sizes for inattention (d = -.66) and hyperactivity/impulsivity (d = -.53), suggesting mindfulness is a promising adjunct — though the authors frame the benefit tentatively.

nodes.label: Spontaneous attentional fluctuations in impaired states and pathological conditions: a neurobiological hypothesis
nodes.summary: The default-mode interference hypothesis: low-frequency default-mode-network activity active during rest can intrude into task periods, producing periodic attentional lapses that compete with goal-directed behaviour — proposed as a cause of performance (reaction-time) variability in ADHD.

nodes.label: Large-scale brain systems in ADHD: beyond the prefrontal-striatal model
nodes.summary: Reframes ADHD away from a single prefrontal-striatal locus toward dysfunction distributed across multiple large-scale resting-state networks (frontoparietal, dorsal attention, motor, visual, default) — a systems-level, non-focal model of the disorder.

nodes.label: Subcortical brain volume differences in participants with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder in children and adults: a cross-sectional mega-analysis
nodes.summary: ENIGMA mega-analysis (1713 ADHD, 1529 controls, 23 sites): several subcortical volumes are smaller in ADHD but with very small effect sizes (Cohen’s d roughly -0.10 to -0.19), largest in children and negligible in adults — real group differences that are far too small to diagnose an individual.

nodes.label: Brain Imaging of the Cortex in ADHD: A Coordinated Analysis of Large-Scale Clinical and Population-Based Samples
nodes.summary: ENIGMA cortical analysis: small surface-area reductions in children with ADHD (largest effect Cohen’s d=-0.21), with no surface-area or thickness differences detected in adolescents or adults — reinforcing that structural imaging is not an individual diagnostic test, least of all in adults.

nodes.label: Shared heritability of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder and autism spectrum disorder
nodes.summary: Review of family, twin and molecular-genetic studies: ADHD and ASD co-occur at high frequency (20–50% of ADHD children meet ASD criteria; 30–80% of ASD children meet ADHD criteria) and family/twin data support partly shared familial-genetic origins, with some candidate pleiotropic genes.

nodes.label: Autism Spectrum Disorders and ADHD: Overlapping Phenomenology, Diagnostic Issues, and Treatment Considerations
nodes.summary: Review of the ASD+ADHD comorbid state: the two share genetic heritability and impairments in social and executive functioning, but differ enough in phenotypic presentation that they are held to be distinct diagnostic categories, and each must be considered when treating the other.

nodes.label: The co-occurrence of autism and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder in children — what do we know?
nodes.summary: Review of ASD–ADHD co-occurrence in children; notes that DSM-IV made an ASD diagnosis an exclusion criterion for ADHD (limiting research), that DSM-5 now permits a dual diagnosis, and that the two share phenotypic features but retain distinct diagnostic criteria.

The same internal restlessness fits ADHD and anxiety equally well
nodes.summary: Held open deliberately. Internal hyperactivity and anxious arousal are near-indistinguishable from the inside, they co-occur often, and depression/stress/sleep produce similar churn. Nothing in the record currently discriminates between them.

nodes.label: The evidence base doesn't obviously generalise to me
nodes.summary: The Horváth sample was 226 university students, 81% women, mean age 21.4, tested online without supervision. The authors themselves caution about generalisability to men and across the lifespan — so the dimensional framing is borrowed, not measured, for my case.

nodes.label: Is ADHD truly dimensional, or does it retain categorical structure?
nodes.summary: The dominant taxometric, quantitative-genetic and impairment evidence favours a continuum, but some taxometric analyses recover categorical structure within ADHD samples (Fassbender 2018) and reviews warn that dimensional thinking can license overdiagnosis (Kazda 2021). A clinically justified action threshold is still required. Held open on purpose.

nodes.label: Is adult-identified ADHD a continuation, a separate syndrome, or a false positive?
nodes.summary: Three birth cohorts found adult and childhood ADHD populations barely overlap, which would make adult ADHD a distinct syndrome. Careful reassessment instead excluded ~95% of screen-positive late-onset cases as better explained by substance use or another disorder, leaving masking-then-late-identification as the reading. All three possibilities bear on a first screening in adulthood, and the record cannot yet distinguish them.

nodes.label: Mind-wandering is impairing but may not be ADHD-specific
nodes.summary: The MEWS shows high sensitivity and specificity for ADHD diagnosis and mind-wandering adds impairment variance beyond core symptoms — yet an independent sample found no ADHD/non-ADHD difference and mind-wandering tracking anxiety instead. Small, underpowered samples on both sides; held open.

nodes.label: The internal state could be internalized hyperactivity or cognitive disengagement — opposite arousal poles
nodes.summary: Two named constructs carve the 'churning inside' feeling in opposite directions. Internalized hyperactivity (Weyandt) is a hyper-aroused, restless, racing pole on the ADHD hyperactivity axis; cognitive disengagement (Becker) is a hypo-aroused, foggy, daydreamy, mentally-slow pole tied to internalizing/depression. They imply different differentials — anxiety on one side, mood on the other — and nothing in the record yet says which the internal state actually is. Held open.

nodes.label: ADHD and anxiety co-occur, but the direction of the relationship is unresolved
nodes.summary: Given how often ADHD and anxiety travel together, three orderings compete: ADHD-driven failure breeds secondary anxiety; anxiety mimics/produces inattention that looks like ADHD; or shared temperament/genetics generate both. Reviews treat the temporal relations as an open substantive question, and the record cannot yet say which applies to the internal state. Held open.

nodes.label: Is emotional dysregulation core to ADHD or a correlated-but-distinct dimension?
nodes.summary: Shaw et al. frame three models that make different predictions: emotion dysregulation and ADHD as correlated but distinct dimensions; emotion dysregulation as a core diagnostic feature of ADHD; or the combination as a separate nosological entity. The evidence does not yet choose between them, which matters here because a foggy/churning internal state might be emotional dysregulation rather than the attentional core.

nodes.label: Self-report and informant accounts disagree, and which to weight is contested
nodes.summary: Sibley et al. found parent report more diagnostically sensitive than self-report, with ADHD adults underreporting and controls overreporting; Kooij et al. note that in adults the patient may actually be the best informant, while a collateral remains of great value. So the evaluation cannot simply trust one source — the discrepancy itself is informative, and the record currently holds only a self-administered screen.

nodes.label: Shared substrate versus distinct categories — where is the ADHD/autism boundary?
nodes.summary: The evidence pulls two ways at once. Genetics and neurocognition point to a partly shared substrate (pleiotropy, shared social/executive deficits), which would favour a common underlying dimension; yet the phenotypes differ enough that the field keeps ADHD and ASD as separate diagnostic categories. Both readings are supported, and this note holds the boundary question open rather than resolving it in either direction.

edges.quote: Adult ADHD was highly comorbid with many other DSM-IV disorders assessed in the survey and was associated with substantial role impairment.
edges.rationale: Verbatim from the MEDLINE abstract (efetch). Nationally representative NCS-R evidence (N=3,199 screened) that adult ADHD travels with other disorders — the empirical basis for the comorbidity being real, not artefactual.

edges.quote: As many as 80% of adults with ADHD have at least one coexisting psychiatric disorder
edges.rationale: Verbatim from the open-access BMC Psychiatry full text (PMC5567978). Puts an upper-bound figure on comorbidity in adults; mood and anxiety are named as the most frequent.

edges.quote: approximately 25% of children with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) exhibit an anxiety disorder
edges.rationale: Verbatim from the MEDLINE abstract (efetch). A specific ADHD–anxiety co-occurrence rate in children, from a review dedicated to the comorbidity.

edges.quote: Studies have concluded that emotional dysregulation is a distinctive attribute of adult ADHD psychopathology
edges.rationale: Verbatim from the PMC full text. Independent support that emotional dysregulation is characteristic of adult ADHD, corroborating Shaw et al.

edges.quote: the conceptualization of ADHD as a spectrum using a dimensional rather than a categorical approach to diagnosis and treatment has been proposed

edges.quote: SCT and ADHD-IN are empirically distinct and correlated more strongly (meta-analytic rs = .63 and .72 in children and adults, respectively) than SCT and ADHD-HI (meta-analytic rs = .32 and .46 in children and adults, respectively).
